source_excerpt:
65% OF NEW GCC JOBS IN INDIA REQUIRE AI SKILLS. THE FUTURE OF WORK IS ALREADY CHANGING. A new report by ANSR, Talent Trends in GCCs in India 2026, carries an important message for India’s students, professionals, educators and employers. 📊 Here are the numbers we cannot afford to ignore: 🔹 Nearly 65% of new GCC roles created in 2026 require AI skills. 🔹 Demand for AI and data professionals has increased by approximately 45% year-on-year. 🔹 GCC hiring grew by around 12–15% year-on-year in the first half of 2026. 🔹 Postings for emerging roles, including Forward Deployed Engineers and AI engineers, have surged dramatically. Source: ANSR, Talent Trends in GCCs in India 2026. But the most important takeaway is not just about the numbers. It is about how we prepare for the jobs of tomorrow. AI is no longer relevant only to computer science graduates. A finance professional who understands AI-powered analytics. A software engineer who can build AI-enabled applications. A cybersecurity specialist who can use intelligent threat detection. A business graduate who can automate workflows and interpret data. Each represents a different way to combine domain expertise with AI capabilities. What does this mean for India’s youth? 1. Learn AI by applying it. Move beyond merely using AI tools. Learn how to solve real problems with them. 2. Combine AI with a domain. AI + Finance. AI + Marketing. AI + Education. AI + Healthcare. AI + Cybersecurity. Your existing knowledge can become more valuable when complemented by AI skills. 3. Build demonstrable capabilities. Projects, portfolios, practical assignments and measurable outcomes can help demonstrate what you can actually do. 4. Develop human skills alongside technical skills. Critical thinking, communication, creativity, ethical judgement and problem-solving remain essential to translating technology into business value. And what does this mean for educational institutions? We must rethink the relationship between education and employability. AI literacy, data fluency, industry projects and experiential learning should not remain optional additions to the curriculum. They must become an integral part of preparing students for a rapidly evolving workplace. It will be realised by people who know how to use technology intelligently. The question for every student, professional and institution is simple: Are we preparing for the jobs that existed yesterday—or developing the capabilities that the world will need tomorrow? The future of employability will belong to those who combine knowledge, skills, adaptability and the ability to work intelligently with AI. #ArtificialIntelligence #FutureOfWork #IndiaJobs #GlobalCapabilityCentres #Upskilling #DigitalSkills #Employability #Education #SkillDevelopment

Huzaifa Khalil Ahmed 3w Report this post AI is no longer the future of work. It is already changing the job market. And Pakistan needs to start paying attention. Recent reporting from India shows that entry-level jobs are already being affected as banks, technology companies and global capability centres increasingly automate routine work that was traditionally given to fresh graduates. This is not just an India problem. It is a South Asian warning. The international market is moving towards a workplace where AI can perform an increasing number of routine tasks faster, cheaper and at scale. So the real question is no longer: “Will AI replace jobs?” The real question is: “Are we preparing our people for the jobs that will exist after AI changes the market?” And honestly, I am worried about Pakistan. Are our students ready? Can they work with AI instead of competing with it? Can they analyse, communicate, solve problems, make decisions and use AI as a productivity tool? Or are we still preparing students primarily to memorise information, pass examinations and enter traditional entry-level roles? Are our universities ready? Adding “AI” to a degree title is not enough. We need curricula that evolve. We need practical projects. We need industry exposure. We need students to understand how AI will transform their own fields. AI + Accounting. AI + Medicine. AI + Law. AI + Engineering The future is not necessarily about everyone becoming an AI engineer. It is about creating AI-capable professionals. Is our government ready? Our policies are only useful when they reach classrooms, workplaces and ordinary students. And then there is the infrastructure question. We are telling students to learn AI, work remotely, freelance globally and compete internationally. But what happens when reliable internet itself is a challenge? What happens when electricity, computing access and digital infrastructure remain inconsistent? How exactly are we expecting our students to compete globally? India is already showing us what early AI-driven disruption can look like. Some tasks will disappear. Some jobs will shrink. Some will be redesigned. New jobs will emerge. And professionals who know how to use AI will potentially become dramatically more productive than those who don't. That creates a very uncomfortable question for Pakistan: What happens when our students spend four years preparing for a job that has already been redesigned by the time they graduate? So I want to ask: Are our students ready? Are our universities ready? Are our teachers ready? Is our government ready? Is our internet infrastructure ready? Or are we simply going to wait until thousands of graduates are unemployed and then say: “We should have prepared earlier.” Because this is not a hypothetical conversation anymore. The warning signs are right in front of us. India is seeing them. The international market is seeing them. Pakistan needs to decide whether it wants to prepare for the change... 3 Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in

vitthal pokalkar 2w Report this post AI Is Taking Jobs. What Does It Mean for India's IT Future? For years, getting a job in the IT industry was a dream for millions of Indian students. For many middle-class families, it meant financial stability, a better lifestyle, and the hope of giving their children a brighter future. Today, that dream is becoming harder to achieve for many young graduates. Artificial intelligence is changing the way software is developed. AI tools can write code, test applications, identify bugs, prepare documentation, and perform tasks that once required hours of human effort. What used to take a team of developers several days can sometimes be completed much faster with the help of AI. This is undoubtedly progress. But there is another side to this story that deserves our attention. If companies can do more work with fewer employees, what happens to the people who depend on those jobs? India's IT industry has created opportunities for generations of engineers and graduates. It has supported families, helped people move into the middle class, and contributed significantly to the country's economic growth. For many young people, an entry-level IT job was the first step towards an independent life. Now, AI is beginning to change the expectations companies have of their employees. Businesses are looking for greater productivity, faster delivery, and lower costs. As AI takes over some routine tasks, companies may need fewer people for certain kinds of work. Fresh graduates could find it particularly difficult to enter the industry if employers expect them to deliver more from their very first day. And this problem is not limited to freshers. Experienced professionals may also have to learn new skills, change roles, or reconsider career paths they spent years building. Of course, software development is not going to disappear overnight. Companies will still need people who understand business problems, design reliable systems, make important technical decisions, protect data, and take responsibility when things go wrong. AI can assist with many tasks, but building useful technology involves much more than writing code. The bigger concern is whether new opportunities will be created quickly enough to replace the work that gets automated.
